svg.aria-label: Diagram: what an Amazon Cognito user pool token asserts, when it stops asserting it, and which revocation operations reach a whole user rather than a single session. The central statement from the revocation documentation is that user pool JSON Web Tokens are self-contained with a signature and expiration time assigned when the token was created, that revoked tokens cannot be used with any Amazon Cognito API calls that require a token, but that revoked tokens will still be valid if they are verified using any JWT library that verifies the signature and expiration of the token. The consequence is that local verification, which fetches the JWKS and checks the RS256 signature along with the expiry, audience and issuer, involves no call to Cognito and therefore cannot observe a revocation, so a revoked token continues to pass verification at a resource server until it expires on its own, which means the effective revocation latency equals the access token lifetime. Three clocks govern lifetime. The ID token expiration can be set to any value between 5 minutes and 1 day, per app client. The access token expiration can likewise be set between 5 minutes and 1 day. The refresh token expires 30 days after sign-in by default and can be configured to any value between 60 minutes and 10 years, so the maximum refresh lifetime of 3,650 days is three thousand six hundred and fifty times the maximum one-day lifetime of an ID or access token, making the refresh token the credential that actually determines how long an account stays usable. Authorisation data travels as claims: the cognito:groups claim is an array of strings naming each user pool group that has the user as a member, and it is always an array even for a single group, so removing a user from a group does not alter any token already issued, because a claim records what was true when the token was signed. A short token life is the obvious mitigation but does not shorten the session, because when a user signs in with managed login Cognito sets session cookies valid for one hour, and specifying a token duration shorter than one hour still leaves the user with a valid session until the cookie expires, during which tokens that expire can be refreshed without the need to reauthenticate. Revocation is keyed on the origin_jti claim, described as a token-revocation identifier associated with the user's refresh token, and when a token is revoked Cognito invalidates all access and ID tokens sharing the same origin_jti value, so revocation operates on a refresh token and its children rather than on a user, and origin_jti is therefore the value to cache if an API must honour revocation. Four operations differ in reach: RevokeToken revokes all access tokens for a given refresh token including the initial access token from interactive sign-in, and does not affect the user's other refresh tokens or their ID and access token children; the revocation endpoint behaves equivalently for a given refresh token and all ID and access tokens that refresh token generated; GlobalSignOut is a self-service operation a user authorizes with their own access token and revokes all of that user's refresh, ID and access tokens, which makes it unsuitable as an offboarding tool; and AdminUserGlobalSignOut is a server-side operation an administrator authorizes with IAM credentials and revokes all of the target user's refresh, ID and access tokens, making it the only operation an administrator can run against a user without holding that user's token. A revocation request must include the client ID that was used to obtain the token. Prerequisites and side effects are recorded: token revocation is enabled by default for a newly created user pool client and refresh tokens can be revoked only in app clients where it is enabled, so a pool predating the feature may have clients where the operation is unavailable; enabling it adds the origin_jti and jti claims to access and ID tokens, which increases their size and can matter where tokens travel in headers; disabling token revocation in a client where it was previously enabled does not make revoked tokens active again; and disabling a user account, which revokes refresh and access tokens, does not reactivate those tokens if the account is later re-enabled. On refresh token rotation, AWS states that rotation reissues a refresh token within the same fixed validity window and does not extend that window, with each new refresh token valid only for the time remaining on the original RefreshTokenValidity period no matter how many times it rotates, illustrated by a 30-day validity where a session rotating daily still expires 30 days after first sign-in rather than 30 days after the most recent rotation, so keeping a user signed in beyond that window requires reauthentication and rotation is a credential-theft control rather than a session-extension mechanism. When rotation is disabled, token-refresh requests return new access and ID tokens only and the original refresh token remains valid, so one stolen refresh token mints working access tokens for the whole window. A grace period of up to 60 seconds can be configured for the original refresh token to allow retries, because concurrent refreshes are a normal pattern. Rotation is incompatible with the REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH authentication flow, which cannot be used in app clients that have rotation enabled, so moving to rotation means moving client code to GetTokensFromRefreshToken and is a migration rather than a toggle. Two parsing cautions are recorded: the set of claims in a Cognito ID token grows over time as new features add claims, so a parser that rejects unexpected claims will eventually break on an AWS feature release, and Cognito generates the sub claim in a Cognito-specific format that does not conform to RFC UUID, so its format should not be strictly validated.
svg.title: Revocation acts on a refresh token and its children; local verification never hears about it
svg.text: “Revoke” is a fact the user pool knows. Your verifier is never told.
Amazon Cognito user pools — what a token asserts, and when it stops.
The sentence that is the whole post
“User pool JWTs are self-contained with a signature and expiration time that was assigned when the token was created.
Revoked tokens can’t be used with any Amazon Cognito API calls that require a token. However, revoked tokens will
still be valid if they are verified using any JWT library that verifies the signature and expiration of the token.”
Local verification — JWKS, RS256, exp, aud, iss — makes no call to Cognito. That is the point of a JWT.
Path A — your resource server
token → JWT authorizer → verify sig + exp → allow
Signature good. exp in the future.
A revoked token passes. Correctly.
Revocation latency = the access token TTL, whatever the runbook says.
Path B — a Cognito API call
token → Cognito → checks origin_jti → refused
“When you revoke a token, Amazon Cognito invalidates
all access and ID tokens with the same origin_jti”
So cache origin_jti, not tokens, if your API must honour it.
Three clocks — and the one that matters is the one nobody reviews
ID token 5 minutes – 1 day per app client
access token 5 minutes – 1 day
refresh token 60 minutes – 10 years default 30 days
365 × 10 = 3,650 days against a 1-day ceiling on the other two — so the refresh token is the real session length.
A group is a claim, not a lookup
“cognito:groups An array of strings. Each string is the
name of a user pool group that has your user as a member”
Remove the user → issued tokens still list the group.
A claim records what was true when the token was signed.
A 5-minute token is not a 5-minute session
managed login sets “session cookies that are valid for
1 hour”
A shorter TTL still leaves “a valid session until the
cookie expires” — refreshed “without the need to
reauthenticate”.
Four operations — only two of them cover a person
RevokeToken one refresh token + children “doesn’t affect any of the user’s other refresh tokens”
Revocation endpoint one refresh token + children same scope
GlobalSignOut ALL of the user’s tokens authorised by the user’s OWN access token
AdminUserGlobalSignOut ALL of the user’s tokens authorised by IAM — the offboarding one
Laptop, phone and CI job = three refresh tokens. And a revoke request “must include the client ID that was used to obtain the token”.
Rotation is theft control, not sliding sessions
“Rotation reissues a refresh token within the same fixed
validity window. It doesn’t extend the window.”
30-day validity, rotating daily → still expires 30 days
after first sign-in. Then: reauthenticate.
Enabling it is a migration, not a toggle
Rotation “isn’t compatible with” REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH
→ client code moves to GetTokensFromRefreshToken
Set the grace period: “up to 60 seconds” — concurrent
refreshes are normal, and one of them otherwise loses.
Revocation state is one-way, deliberately: disabling the feature, or re-enabling a disabled user, does not bring revoked tokens back.
And enabling revocation adds origin_jti + jti, which “increase the size of” the tokens — they travel in headers, and headers have limits.
